Alongside sequences and logarithms, AA SL's syllabus explicitly examines simple deductive proof: the ability to construct a short chain of logical steps from agreed premises to a stated conclusion, and to recognise when a single counterexample is enough to destroy a general claim.

label.en: ● Mathematical proof: direct proof, exhaustion & counterexample (AA SL)

body.en:
Direct proof starts from a definition or an already-established result and reasons forward, step by justified step, to the claim. A standard opening move: write an even integer as \(2k\) and an odd integer as \(2k+1\) for some integer \(k\), then manipulate algebraically.

Proof by exhaustion is only valid when the claim can be split into a *finite* number of cases that together cover every possibility (e.g. checking all residues mod \(n\)) — each case is then verified separately.

Disproof by counterexample is the standard way to show a universal statement ("for all \(n\), …") is false: exhibiting one value of \(n\) for which it fails is a complete, rigorous disproof — no further argument is needed, and no number of confirming cases can substitute for it if a single counterexample exists.

problem.en: Prove that the sum of any two consecutive odd integers is divisible by 4.

solution.en:
Let the two consecutive odd integers be \(2k+1\) and \(2k+3\) for some integer \(k\).

Their sum is \((2k+1)+(2k+3)=4k+4=4(k+1).\)

Since \(k+1\) is an integer, \(4(k+1)\) is a multiple of 4. Hence the sum of any two consecutive odd integers is divisible by 4. ∎

problem.en: Ahmad claims: "for every positive integer \(n\), \(n^2+n+41\) is prime." Show this claim is false.

solution.en:
The formula does produce primes for many small values of \(n\) (e.g. \(n=1\) gives 43, a prime) — but checking many cases can never prove a "for all \(n\)" claim, only a single failure can disprove it.

Take \(n=40\): \(n^2+n+41=40^2+40+41=1600+40+41=1681=41^2.\)

Since \(1681=41\times41\) is composite, \(n=40\) is a counterexample. The claim is false. ∎

body.en:
Prove that the square of any integer is either a multiple of 4 or one more than a multiple of 4.

Solution: Every integer \(n\) is either even or odd — a finite, exhaustive split into two cases.

Case 1 (even): \(n=2k \Rightarrow n^2=4k^2\), a multiple of 4.

Case 2 (odd): \(n=2k+1 \Rightarrow n^2=4k^2+4k+1=4(k^2+k)+1\), one more than a multiple of 4.

Both cases are covered, so the statement holds for every integer. ∎

body.en:
An arithmetic sequence has first term \(a\) and common difference \(d\). The 6th term is 17 and the sum of the first 8 terms is 88. Find \(a\) and \(d\).

Show solution

\(u_6=a+5d=17\)  (1)

\(S_8=\frac{8}{2}(2a+7d)=88\Rightarrow 2a+7d=22\)  (2)

From (1): \(a=17-5d.\) Sub into (2): \(2(17-5d)+7d=22\Rightarrow 34-3d=22\Rightarrow d=4.\)

\(a=17-20=-3.\)  Answer: \(a=-3,\;d=4.\)

Find the 8th term and sum of the first 8 terms of the sequence 3, 6, 12, …

Solution: \(u_1=3,\; r=2\)

\(u_8 = 3 \cdot 2^{7} = 384\)

\(S_8 = \dfrac{3(2^8-1)}{2-1} = 3\times 255 = 765\)
